function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact contents of the files that will be created/updated so you can verify them before committing.

> **NOTE** – I’m assuming the repository is a standard Node.js project that exposes an HTTP API on port 3000.  
> If your app uses a different port or has special build steps, tweak the files accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

> In a real‑world scenario you could run a script that scans the source tree and decides on the best Docker base image, ports, etc.  
> For this exercise I’ll hand‑craft the artefacts based on a typical Node.js project.

### 2.1 Create / update `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official Node.js LTS image as the base
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only production dependencies, keeping the image lean.  
> * The app is assumed to start with `npm start` and listen on port 3000.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

Create a new directory `k8s` and add the following file:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- adjust if you use another registry
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # Service port
      targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 3 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80 (you can change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).  
> * Uses the image tag `latest`; you can replace it with a specific tag if you prefer.

### 2.3 Create GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Update deployment image
        uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v3
        with:
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
        # Optional: if you want to automatically roll out the new image
        # run: |
        #   kubectl set image deployment/nodejs-welcome-deployment nodejs-welcome=ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Key points**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Installs dependencies, runs tests, builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
> * The last step is optional – you can uncomment it if you want the workflow to automatically update the Kubernetes deployment.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
# Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally (optional)
docker build -t nodejs-welcome-test .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests apply locally (requires a cluster)
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes images on `main` pushes |

Feel free to tweak the image registry, tags, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
